_note: The atlas glossary. Copy strings mark a term as [[id|text]]; pages show the short definition and its example on hover and focus, and link here. learning_order lists the core terms in the order a newcomer meets them; the glossary page shows those first, then every term A to Z. Plain words, no em dashes.

terms.short: A language and program for writing mathematical statements and proofs, then verifying each proof step. A verified proof establishes the statement as written; comparing that statement and its definitions with a paper is a separate task.
terms.example: PiExponent is a Lean file stating that the irrationality exponent of π is 2.

terms.short: OpenAI’s group of related papers about a main result. Each group has a number in its catalogue; Atlas uses that number to link the papers and reports about them.
terms.example: Family 017, “The irrationality exponent of π is 2”, holds one paper and one Lean statement, PiExponent.

terms.short: The main claim OpenAI’s catalogue gives for a family. A family’s Lean statements may state all of it, part of it, or a supporting step.
terms.example: Family 017’s headline makes two claims: π’s irrationality exponent is 2, and the Flint–Hills series converges.

terms.short: A file stating a theorem in Lean, usually with sorry in place of its proof (Comparator calls it a challenge file). Comparator’s settings identify the statement to verify, the definitions the proof may supply and the axioms it may use. OpenAI provides its proof separately.
terms.example: PiExponent.lean states the exponent of π as the theorem OAI.PiExponent.main, with sorry where the proof would go.

terms.short: A program that tests OpenAI’s separate proof against a Lean statement. Acceptance means that Lean’s proof verifier accepts the configured theorem using only the allowed axioms. It does not establish that the statement means the same thing as a paper’s theorem.
terms.example: MathVet and cert-machine each report that Comparator accepted OpenAI’s proof of PiExponent.

terms.short: Lean’s placeholder for a missing proof. A Lean statement leaves its proof as sorry on purpose; the proof is in OpenAI’s separate solution module.
terms.example: The theorem in PiExponent.lean ends with by sorry.

terms.short: The axioms a configuration allows a proof to use, here the three standard ones: propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. A replay shows which ones a proof actually uses.
terms.example: PiExponent’s configuration allows propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice.

terms.short: A definition a configuration lists for the solution to supply. Comparator compares it by name and type only, so its body comes from the solution and must be read there.
terms.example: PiExponent’s configuration lists no definition holes, so every definition it uses is compared as written.

terms.short: The small core of Lean that checks every step of a proof. Everything Lean accepts passes through it.
terms.example: cert-machine reports that Lean’s kernel and nanoda both accept OpenAI’s proof of PiExponent.

terms.short: A second proof-verification program for Lean, written independently in Rust. Comparator can run it alongside Lean’s own verifier. The report for each run states which verifiers were used when that information is available.
terms.example: cert-machine ran PiExponent through Comparator with nanoda switched on and recorded “CERTIFIED”.

terms.short: The community-maintained library of mathematical definitions, theorems and proofs written in Lean. OpenAI’s release specifies the version it uses.
terms.example: PiExponent writes π as Mathlib’s Real.pi.

terms.short: OpenAI’s note on what a family’s Lean statements cover, in lean/docs of the release. The atlas quotes it beside other people’s readings.
terms.example: OpenAI’s note for family 017 says: “The paper’s convergence consequence for the Flint–Hills series is outside this selected statement.”

terms.short: A group’s attempt to verify OpenAI’s proof with Comparator, sometimes called a re-run. Atlas records the group’s reported result and the release version used. Atlas has not repeated the runs.
terms.example: MathVet’s Comparator run of PiExponent, which it reports as “comparator-sandboxed-pass”.

terms.short: MathVet and Carlos Toledo’s cert-machine, the two outside groups that each read every family’s Lean statements against its headline, independently of OpenAI and of each other, under their own published rules. Each states its own method; the atlas quotes their verdicts and notes and adds none of its own.
terms.example: For family 017 MathVet says “full” and cert-machine says “NARROWER — DECLARED”, and both notes name the missing Flint–Hills claim.

terms.short: A proof assistant separate from Lean. Ben Knill’s reports use it to prove selected steps in some of the release’s papers. They also test deliberately incorrect examples that the program should reject.
terms.example: Ben Knill’s HOL Light card for family 017 checks that the Flint–Hills partial sum up to n = 355 exceeds 24.

terms.short: A calculation that decides a finite claim using exact arithmetic or exhaustive enumeration, implemented independently of the paper. A successful calculation establishes the specific tested property. An undecided result is not evidence that the claim is false.

A possible link between a paper statement and a Lean statement, also called a candidate pairing. It comes from a citation in the Lean source, from a source reading, or from words the two statements share. No person has reviewed that their mathematical meanings agree.
terms.example: Atlas shows Theorem 1.1 of the π paper as PiExponent’s possible match, from words the two share, such as pi, integer and real.

terms.short: The atlas’s HTML version of a paper, converted from its TeX at the pinned commit. The PDF stays the reference; a page that did not convert in full lists what is missing.
terms.example: The π paper’s reading page shows Theorem 1.1 with a link to its line in the TeX source.

terms.short: A paper OpenAI removed after the release, with a notice explaining the gap. The atlas keeps it, marked, under the family it was listed in on release day.
terms.example: “Algebraicity of Kuga-Satake Correspondences for K3 Surfaces”, kept in family 032.

terms.short: A paper OpenAI later replaced with a revised edition. The atlas keeps the earlier edition, marked, beside the current one in the same family.
terms.example: An earlier edition of “A pointwise 2-converse for elliptic curves with rational two-torsion”, kept beside its revision in family 004.

terms.short: One of the two outside groups. It reads each family’s Lean statements against the headline under a published rubric, with help from a model, and runs Comparator itself. Its verdict and note are quoted in its own terms.
terms.example: For family 017 MathVet says “full”, and its note adds that the Flint–Hills corollary is not stated.

terms.short: Carlos Toledo’s audit of the release, one of the two outside groups. It re-runs every Lean statement through Comparator with nanoda switched on, reads each family’s Lean statements against the headline clause by clause, and decides finite parts of some papers with exact code.
terms.example: For family 017 cert-machine says “NARROWER — DECLARED”: the Flint–Hills claim is in the headline but not in PiExponent, and OpenAI’s note says so.

terms.short: Definitions written in the Lean statement file, in addition to those imported from Mathlib. To judge whether the statement means the same thing as a paper theorem, compare these definitions with the paper as well.

With no citation and no source reading, Statement Map, the program that collects Atlas’s records, selects a possible paper match by comparing words in the Lean statement with every statement in the family, and pairs one only when the match is clear. No person has reviewed that their mathematical meanings agree.
terms.example: PiExponent is matched to Theorem 1.1 of its paper this way.

terms.term: Paired from the catalogue’s words, as a fallback
terms.short: Earlier releases of Atlas’s records fell back to words in OpenAI’s catalogue description when the Lean wording gave no clear match. Since reader v9 (26 October 2026) this fallback is not used: nothing is paired instead.

No citation, source reading or clear word match links the Lean statement to one paper statement, so nothing is paired. When an AI agent read both sources and found no counterpart, its reason is shown.

terms.term: Paired by a citation in the Lean
terms.short: The Lean source cites a paper statement, and Atlas records that citation. Atlas records no review that the statements mean the same thing.

terms.term: Paired by the release’s own declaration
terms.short: OpenAI’s release explicitly links the Lean statement to a paper statement. Atlas records that link, with no recorded review that the statements mean the same thing.
The map’s colours compare the two groups’ assessments of each family’s Lean statements. They do not say whether a paper’s proof is correct.
terms.example: A family whose groups disagree, like family 017 (“full” against “NARROWER — DECLARED”), is coloured to show the disagreement.

terms.short: A record by a named reader, so far always an AI agent (recorded as Codex source review 1 to 4), who read a Lean statement’s source and the paper and noted which Lean declaration states which paper statement, how the two relate and what the link leaves out. It compares statements, not proofs, and no person has reviewed it.
terms.example: A source reading records that ErdosReciprocal and Corollary 1.2 of its paper state the same claim.
